title: Rust Dojo
description: Duolingo-style Rust lessons. All lesson content lives in this JSON file.

units.title: Unit 1 - Getting Started
units.description: Output, variables, and the basic types.

exercises.prompt: What does this macro call do?
options: Prints Hello, world! followed by a newline
Prints Hello, world! with no newline
exercises.explanation: println! prints its arguments to stdout and appends a newline (\n).

exercises.prompt: Which macro prints text WITHOUT adding a trailing newline? Type the macro name, including the exclamation mark.
exercises.explanation: print! writes exactly what you give it. println! is the one that adds the newline.

exercises.prompt: Every binary Rust program must define a fn main() function.
exercises.explanation: main is the entry point the runtime calls to start your program.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword makes a let binding reassignable?
exercises.explanation: Bindings are immutable by default; mut makes one mutable, so `let mut x = 4;`.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the missing keyword so the constant compiles.
exercises.explanation: const declares a compile-time constant. It must have an explicit type.

exercises.prompt: Shadowing with a new let can change the type of a name.
exercises.explanation: Unlike mut reassignment, `let x = "text";` can shadow an integer x and change its type.

exercises.prompt: What integer type does an unannotated integer literal default to?
exercises.explanation: Integer literals default to i32 unless inference or an annotation says otherwise.

exercises.prompt: Which type can hold the value -1?
exercises.explanation: Only signed types (i8, i16, ...) can hold negatives. u-types are zero and positive only.

exercises.prompt: In Rust, 'a' is a char and "a" is a &str.
exercises.explanation: Single quotes make a char (one Unicode scalar value); double quotes make a string slice.

exercises.prompt: Complete the array type for five i32 values.
exercises.explanation: An array type is written [element type; length], e.g. [i32; 5].

units.title: Unit 2 - Input & Math
units.description: Read from the user and do arithmetic safely.

exercises.prompt: Complete the import so you can use stdin.
exercises.explanation: `use std::io;` brings the io module into scope so you can write io::stdin().

exercises.prompt: Which line reads a line of text from the user?
exercises.explanation: read_line appends into a &mut String and returns a Result.

exercises.prompt: read_line removes the trailing newline from the input.
exercises.explanation: It keeps the newline, which is why you usually call .trim() before using the value.

exercises.prompt: What is the result of this integer division?
exercises.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero, discarding the fractional part.

exercises.prompt: What keyword converts a numeric type explicitly?
exercises.template: let z = x ___ f32 / y as f32;
exercises.explanation: `as` performs an explicit cast. Rust never converts numeric types implicitly.

exercises.prompt: In a debug build, what happens on integer overflow?
exercises.code:
let a: u8 = 255;
let b = a + 1;
exercises.explanation: Debug builds panic on overflow. Release builds wrap around (two's complement).

exercises.prompt: Rust will automatically convert an i16 to an i32 when you add them.
exercises.explanation: There are no implicit numeric conversions; you must cast with `as` yourself.

units.title: Unit 3 - Control Flow
units.description: Make decisions, repeat work, and reuse code.

exercises.prompt: What type must an if condition have?
exercises.explanation: Conditions must be bool. There is no truthy/falsy coercion in Rust.

exercises.prompt: Complete the if expression.
exercises.explanation: `if ... { } else { }` is an expression here; both arms must have the same type.

exercises.prompt: In Rust, if is an expression, so it can produce a value.
exercises.explanation: That is why `let x = if c { 1 } else { 2 };` works.

exercises.prompt: Which loop can break with a value, making the whole loop evaluate to it?
exercises.explanation: Only `loop` supports `break value;` because the compiler knows it can only exit via break.

exercises.prompt: How many numbers does this half-open range yield? (type a number)
exercises.explanation: 1..5 is half-open: 1, 2, 3, 4 = four values. Use 1..=5 for five.

exercises.prompt: What does continue do inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of this iteration and starts the next
Returns a value from the loop
exercises.explanation: continue jumps to the next iteration; break leaves the loop.

exercises.prompt: What symbol separates a function's parameters from its return type?
exercises.template: fn add(a: i32, b: i32) ___ i32 { a + b }
exercises.explanation: The arrow `->` gives the return type. No arrow means the return type is ().

exercises.prompt: Adding a trailing semicolon to the last expression returns that value.
exercises.explanation: The semicolon turns the expression into a statement, so the function returns () - a type error.

exercises.prompt: How do you return more than one value from a function?
exercises.explanation: Return a tuple like (min, max) and destructure it at the call site.

units.title: Unit 4 - Deep Rust
units.description: Ownership and modelling your own data.

exercises.prompt: After this move, can you still use s?
options: No - s was moved into t
Yes - t is just an alias
exercises.explanation: String owns heap memory and is not Copy. Assignment moves it, invalidating s.

exercises.prompt: You can hold several &T shared borrows and a &mut T at the same time.
exercises.explanation: You may have many shared borrows OR one exclusive borrow, never both at once.

exercises.prompt: Complete the mutable reference so the function can modify the string.
exercises.explanation: &mut T is an exclusive (read/write) reference. The source value must also be mut.

exercises.prompt: Which of these types is Copy (so assignment copies instead of moving)?
exercises.explanation: Scalars like i32 implement Copy. String and Vec own heap data and are move-only.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword defines a group of named fields?
exercises.explanation: `struct` groups named fields into one type.

exercises.prompt: In an impl block, which method receiver CONSUMES the value?
exercises.explanation: `self` takes ownership, so the value cannot be used afterwards. &self borrows to read, &mut self borrows to modify.

exercises.prompt: A match expression must handle every variant of the enum it matches on.
exercises.explanation: match is exhaustive; the compiler forces you to cover all cases (or add a _ arm).
